Coronary angiography showed normal coronary arteries and the echocardiogram was normal without regional wall-motion abnormalities or a significant effusion. Acute pericarditis is supported by chest pain + characteristic ECG changes (2 of the diagnostic criteria); elevated inflammatory markers further support an inflammatory pericardial process. The troponin rise indicates myocardial involvement (myopericarditis) rather than an occlusive coronary infarction; a normal cath essentially excludes an acute thrombotic STEMI. Primary myocarditis remains a possibility (can present with chest pain, troponin elevation, inflammatory markers, and often normal coronaries) but the highly specific ECG pattern of PR depression and diffuse ST elevation favors pericardial involvement. Other considerations that can mimic this presentation (but are less likely given the data) include coronary vasospasm (transient ST elevations with normal cath if spasm has resolved), pulmonary embolism (can cause troponin rise but not the PR-depression/ST-elevation pattern), and less likely aortic pathology or esophageal rupture given demographics and normal exam/echo.

DIAGNOSIS:
1. Acute viral pericarditis with myocardial involvement (myopericarditis)
2. Acute myocarditis (viral)
3. Acute coronary syndrome (STEMI/non-STEMI) — resolved thrombus or nonobstructive MI (less likely given normal coronary angiography)
4. Coronary vasospasm (Prinzmetal angina) with transient ST-elevation
5. Pulmonary embolism causing right-heart strain and troponin elevation
